subtopic: MR. KNOWLES-PEGGING OF OLD AGE SECURITY PENSIONS TO COST OF LIVING INDEX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege affecting not only all the members of this house but more than a million Canadians. It may be that my point of privilege is due to a misprint in a document which I have in my hand. If so that can be corrected without delay. On the other hand, if what I have in my hand is correct I think other steps should be taken. Yesterday in the course of her remarks to this house the Minister of National Health and Welfare used these words:
-all future old age security pensions will be pegged to the cost of living index and will increase automatically if living costs increase.
Later she said:
-this will provide not only a greater measure of security but will also protect the real value of the pension dollar for Canada's million-odd pensioners.
We were given no details, but what the minister said was spoken in the present tense. When we got the bill last night after the debate was over we learned that the possible increase due to this adjustment cannot be received by any person drawing old age security until 1968, and that the possible amount of increase in 1968 is 75 cents.

Mr. Speaker, on the particular point I should hasten to say to the
chamber that this is not a misprint; that the address I made yesterday was on the resolution preceding Bill No. C-136, and this was known by all hon. members to be the case. All the remarks I made at that time have reference to that particular bill. Since last August it has been known by the members of this chamber and members of the public that the initial coming into effect of the bill was not anticipated to be until January 1, 1966. Within the bill there is provision for commencement, on a number of dates subsequent to that date, of benefits which will accrue to contributors and survivors; that also in the bill is indicated the initial tying to an index figure, something to take into account the increases, if any, which take place over a certain period of time which are then calculated for a two year period. There was no attempt to mislead the chamber or the public at large; that the amendments to the old age security act which are incorporated as part of Bill C-136 would come into effect at any point of time earlier than the main provisions of the Canada pension plan.
In so far as my hon. friend's suggestion that the original increase would be 75 cents or $1.50, it should be noted that use of an index is a departure, and it is the first time an index has been used for any payment in this country. My hon. friend and his party, as well as other hon. members opposite, enthusiastically accepted this last night, and indeed have heretofore urged such an inclusion in government legislation. My hon. friend now sounds as if he is unhappy that one of the matters which he himself has urged has been adopted by the government.
It should not be forgotten that the index which is to be attached to the old age security payments is to bring them into line with the index which is attached to pension payments under the Canada pension plan proper. Nothing in the proposed old age security amendments deals with the base rate of $75 a month which this government introduced a year ago and which was unanimously approved by the house. Nor is anything in this bill intended to exclude any future action by any parliament with respect to that base.
This is a very major, very far reaching and sweeping change in social legislation in this country, Mr. Speaker, and indeed commences

Question of Privilege
in a responsible way by tying the plan to the index at the time at which it comes into operation. I suppose my hon. friend in the flush of yesterday's by-election victory, which he should regard really as a victory against the Conservative party and not otherwise, now seeks to make political capital out of something which he has generously, and I think sincerely, long since accepted as a really major step forward. I would ask my hon. friend and all hon. members of the house to bear in mind that in the usual spirit of Canadian fiscal responsibility we are beginning this experiment in a relatively modest manner.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF INCREASES IN PENSIONS AND ALLOWANCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 30 I informed the house that there would be an announcement of government proposals to increase pensions and war veterans allowances. In conformity with that statement I am now able to make the following announcement.
There will be brought before the house at the earliest opportunity a supplementary estimate that will enable an across the board increase in disability pensions payable under the Pension Act of approximately 10 per cent, and a similar increase to pensions awarded to widows and dependent children. I am sure the house will agree that this increase in pension rates is warranted.
I am pleased to announce that the supplementary estimates will include an amount which will permit an increase in the attendance allowance from the present maximum of $1,800 a year to a maximum $3,000 a year. There will also be increases in the allowances such as for wear and tear of clothing, which are also authorized by the

Pension Act under certain circumstances. It is estimated that the additional annual cost of these pension increases, based on the present number of pensioners, will be about $17 million, and the annual cost of increasing the attendance allowance will be some $500,000.
The other important matter to which I wish to refer is the proposal of the government to increase war veterans allowances. In reaching a decision on the appropriate amount of these increases we have taken into consideration the recommendations that have been made by veterans organizations. It is proposed to increase the maximum monthly rate of war veterans allowances for a single person to $94 and for a person paid at the married rate to $161 a month, with corresponding adjustments in the rates paid to orphans.
In considering appropriate adjustments in the maximum income ceilings under the War Veterans Allowance Act we have also considered the recommendations received from organized veterans. We have decided that any adjustments in the ceilings should remove the anomaly that at present exists with respect to the ceiling applicable to veterans and widows below age 70 and the ceiling above age 70, where the recipient is in receipt of an old age security pension. At present a recipient over that age is in effect allowed a ceiling, if payment is at the single rate, of $240 a year higher than if he or she were under age 70 and, if payment is at the married rate and the husband and wife are both over age 70, the difference is $480 a year.
In order to provide a ceiling in accordance with the recommendations we have received, and to remove this anomaly, but nevertheless ensure that every recipient will enjoy some increase, including the proposed disability pension increase, we are proposing that the annual income ceilings be raised to $1,596 for a single recipient and to $2,664 where the recipient is paid at the married rate.
I should also mention that corresponding increases in rates and changes in income ceilings will apply as well to those who are in receipt of allowances under the Civilian War Pensions and Allowances Act. These increases and changes under both acts will also be accomplished by means of a supplementary estimate. It is estimated that these proposed increases in rates and the ceiling adjustments under the War Veterans Allowance Act and the Civilian War Pensions and Allowances Act will result in an additional expenditure of about $16,250,000 a year.
Veterans Pensions Increase
I am sure, Mr. Speaker, this statement will be welcomed by members of the house as an indication of the recognition that the welfare of Canada's veterans is of responsible concern to all of us.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at what I consider to be the invitation of the Prime Minister yesterday with respect to making a motion to adjourn the house under standing order 26, I do so now in the light of the evident failure of the government to take the responsibility that is properly theirs by placing before the house the whole of the affairs surrounding the activities of the trustees of the maritime union; surrounding the circumstances of the departure from Canada of Mr. Banks and the failure of the government law agencies of Canada to locate him; the circumstances surrounding allegations made in national press articles which implicate Liberal members of parliament and the Liberal government as a whole, implications which if they are well founded may well cause the seats that those members are holding to be occupied improperly. I believe, under the provisions of the Canada Elections Act, that if offences have been committed of the nature implied in these articles, then the seats of these members today are void.
Motion for Adjournment
The tentacles of Mr. Banks and the S.I.U. seem to be involving ever more Liberal members of parliament. The most recent one, and the case which I think underlines the need for an urgent and immediate study of this problem by the government, is that of the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Basford) who was implicated by name and by riding in a news broadcast this morning. Since lunch time that hon. member has given an interview to Vancouver radio station CKNW and admitted that he had in fact received help from the S.I.U. This was following a story yesterday by CKNW reporter Ed Murphy. He is the first Liberal member who has had the courage to come forward and admit his complicity. This in itself emphasizes the need for a detailed and immediate investigation into such situations.
I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Woolliams)-

Mr. Speaker, may I deal with a question which was raised yesterday and previously, and make a statement about parole in the cases of commuted death sentences both in regard to what is known as the Meeker case and in the wider context of such cases generally.
I can now inform the house that the government proposes to take steps for the enactment of a regulation under the Parole Act which will have the effect of providing that every person who is serving a sentence of imprisonment, to which a sentence of death has been commuted, shall in no case be released on parole without the prior approval of the governor in council. subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION

speechtext: The house resumed, from Tuesday, October 20, consideration in committee of Bill No. C-72, to provide for the establishment of electoral boundaries commissions to report upon the readjustment of the representation of the provinces in the House of Commons and to provide for the readjustment of such

representation in accordance therewith-Mr. Pickersgill (for Mr. Pearson)-Mr. Lamou-reux in the chair.
On clause 6-Appointment of chairman.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
When the committee rose on October 20 it had reverted to a consideration of clause 6, with an amendment thereto by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. The other outstanding clauses are 7, 8, 9, 12 and 13.
Is the committee ready for the question on the amendment to clause 6?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: I should like to say a word or two before we vote on this amendment, if that is the desire of the committee. I know it is not strictly in order but perhaps you would permit me, Mr. Chairman, to say that I was very much impressed by the progress which has been made during my absence- wondering, perhaps, whether I should not have stayed away longer-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: You have taken the words out of my mouth.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
My colleague the Minister of Labour seemed to do so well the other day when this measure was before the committee. But I am hoping that the spirit induced by the hon. gentleman will carry over to our proceedings this afternoon. I think hon. members will recall that at the time we suspended discussion on clause 6 of the bill last April there had developed what might really be regarded as the only serious difference which has yet arisen with regard to this legislation. I should like to recall to hon. members in all quarters of the committee the spirit in which this legislation was approached. I think here I can speak for the government, although in most respects it is clearly understood that once the principle of this bill was adopted, there were no whips on it and every hon. member as far as this side of the house was concerned was considered in every way free, just as was the case the last time a similar measure was before the house, to vote in any way he pleased without any concern because the position of the government was not en jeu then, and is not now. This is a matter for the house, one in which all of us have an equal responsibility. I am, therefore, very conscious of the fact that I can speak only for myself except in one respect: I think I can say it is the view of the government that because of the far reaching, revolutionary character of this legislation it is preferable

that it be accomplished by a consensus rather than by sharp differences and votes.
It is true, as the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre pointed out, the last day when I was present in this committee when we previously discussed this matter, that there was a division over the question as to whether there should be one commission for the whole country or ten commissions. But there was no acrimony attached to the debate on that matter and there was the readiest acceptance of the view that once a reasonable discussion had taken place the question should be decided by the majority of votes in the committee. I hope this will be the spirit in the committee today. I did indicate during the last few days of April when this subject was being discussed that I personally was more inclined-"more disposed" was the phrase I used-to support the amendment of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre than I was to support the original provision in the bill. At the risk of repetition I should like to put on record again the words I used on that occasion, words which will be found at page 2320 of Hansard. I said then:
If the house decided to accept the bill in its present form I would not waste any tears on the amendment. In fact, I would have a certain amount of satisfaction, but I really do believe we would have a better act with this amendment. Because all those in the country are not Liberals and Conservatives-
Perhaps I can say that today without dissent, at any rate from one comer of the house.
-because all those in the country perhaps have not got the same highminded view of the Leader of the Opposition and the Prime Minister as those of us in the house have, I think there would be a greater degree of general confidence in the commissions if we were to accept the amendment that has been proposed than if we were to take the bill in its present form. For that reason I am disposed to support the amendment.
Since that time I have not changed my view. But I cannot ignore the fact that the amendment of the hon. gentleman did arouse very strong antagonism in one part of the committee. I did not myself think that the antagonism was justified, but this is a free country and a free assembly. It was a fact. During the past four or five weeks while unable to be here to take part in the work of the house I have been pondering other possible ways of dealing with this matter. I wish to emphasize what I said on second reading and what I have said at every stage -that while we produced the best bill we were able to draft, we were prepared to accept from any quarter of the house any suggestion for improvement. That still goes.
Electoral Boundaries Commissions By "improvement" I do not just mean something which is academically better. I use the term to include something which is more generally acceptable to the whole house as long as it meets the basic requirements of the legislation.
I was somewhat impressed by having recalled to my mind the suggestion made in a bill introduced by Senator Power when he was in this house many years ago. It was not proceeded with because of the war, but in that bill there was a provision for the Speaker to make these appointments after consultation with certain hon. members in the house. I have been rather impressed by both parts of this suggestion and while I was elsewhere and not otherwise occupied I prepared two draft amendments about which I should like to say something-I have some copies, and when I get to them I will be glad to pass them around to hon. members so that they can read them. I am not going to move them now. I could not do so, in any case, because there is an amendment before the committee now. But so that we can take a general look at the whole question, before doing that

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: May I suggest to the hon. gentleman that he pass them around now and let us look at them. Don't keep them secret.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: I have not the capacity of the right hon. gentleman for holding the attention of an audience; I would prefer not to make a distraction available. I would rather have hon. members listen to what I have to say until I get to that point. I know I need the assistance of the right hon. gentleman in making my speeches much more than he is in need of assistance from me, but I would really prefer to make my own.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: I thought the hon. gentleman wanted co-operation, and we were giving him co-operation. I was trying to secure it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: The right hon. gentleman is correct. But I do not spell "co-operation" "d-i-c-t-a-t-i-o-n". I hope the right hon. gentleman will not take the view that unless we agree with him there is no co-operation in the house.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
A statement like that is quite in keeping with what we expect from the hon. gentleman. We have tried to practise co-operation. He claimed a moment ago that this was the desire. A moment ago I made the suggestion in the best of good spirits, but the hon. gentleman is continuing

Electoral Boundaries Commissions the attitude he has taken previously with regard to the C.B.C.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I think the right hon. gentleman is quite right. I think I have behaved quite badly, and I apologize.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I wonder whether the hon. gentleman would answer a question.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: Certainly.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: He said, "the Speaker, in consultation with certain members". I wonder whether he would now outline the members he has in mind. That would come to grips with the subject immediately.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman. I hope the hon. gentleman will not think this is offensive-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: No.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
-but I would prefer to deal with this matter in the way that I think will make clear what I am hoping to make clear about a rather complicated subject. In other words, it is perhaps almost out of order for me to be doing what I am doing now, because we are really supposed to be discussing nothing but the amendment of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. It is perhaps almost a discourtesy to him, for which I should perhaps apologize, to be suggesting that it ought to be supplanted with something else. But I would like first of all to say a little more about the hon. gentleman's own amendment. There was one objection to it which was made by hon. members in certain quarters of the house and which I thought had some substance. That was, that apart from the representation commissioner, all three members of the commissions would be appointed by the same person. It is true that there were limitations on the kind of persons who could be appointed, but notwithstanding that fact, that is perhaps rather a concentration of power in the hands of one man, even though that man is the chief justice of the province.
Therefore it seemed to me that if we could find some other way to diffuse this power of appointment in some way that would be acceptable to the whole house, it ought to be done. One of the suggestions that I am going to put forward is that if the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre was willing to withdraw his amendment, or if his motion should not be accepted by the committee when it is voted upon, we should then accept an amendment which would

substitute appointment by His Honour the Speaker for the appointment by the leaders of the two major parties in the house. In support of that I could quote a number of-

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: From categories, or just anybody?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
My own view is that of course that would be a possibility; but I would think that after the debate we have had, in the light of all the experience, which is bound to be followed to some degree, in other commonwealth countries, and in view of the difficulty that the hon. gentleman himself recognized in his amendment, namely that these categories of persons referred to are not civil servants of the federal state but are provincial civil servants or persons in other categories whom we cannot order, it might be much better to trust His Honour the Speaker to do the sensible thing, and not to put any strings upon him except the obvious string that these appointments must be made from persons resident in the province.
In the course of the debate hon. gentlemen made a number of points. The hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings said, as reported at page 2291 of Hansard:
We have a Prime Minister who is an officer of the house and a Leader of the Opposition who is also an officer of the house, and they are the only ones in this category. I agree that whoever occupied the office of prime minister or leader of the opposition would exercise the authority given to them under this provision in a manner which would be entirely creditable both to themselves and to parliament-
I think that will always be true. The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, as recorded at page 2298 of Hansard, said this:
X think the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre should correct his stand on this. What is required in this country is respect for parliament, and that carries with it respect for the leaders of these two great parties.
The hon. member said a little later on:
Obviously some people in the left hand corner of the chamber have no respect for the leader of the Liberal party or the leader of the Conservative party, but there are millions of people in the country who have, while their supporters are not very numerous.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: It has changed since then.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
One could make some comments on that. The hon. member for Edmonton West said:
I would say to the Minister of Justice that in discussing the qualifications, capabilities or impartiality of the Prime Minister or the Leader of the Opposition, one must not consider the personalities of the right hon. gentlemen who are

now occupying those positions. If you do this, you may be merely legislating for the next five years.
Then he went on to suggest that the amendment of the hon. gentleman was an implied reflection on the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition acting in a responsible manner as officers of the house and a reflection that they would not do a proper job. I could quote several other hon. members. There is a quotation of the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary as reported at page 2307 of Hansard-I am not going to read it -and several other hon. gentlemen opposite. The gist of all this is the same, namely that we should have confidence that whoever is the prime minister, whoever is the leader of the government, whoever is the leader of the opposition, would make proper appointments. I believe this would be true. But I also share a good deal of the feelings of hon. gentlemen in the other corner of the house who do not support either of these hon. gentlemen and who have pointed out, quite properly I think, that both the occupants of these offices are now, and as long as we have free government will continue to be, politicians.
If, however, hon. gentlemen opposite really believe what they said-and I do not say they do not; I believe they do-about the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition acting in this capacity, surely all of us in every quarter of the house would at all times be ready to trust the one officer of this house elected by us all, who is called the Speaker of the House of Commons because he is our voice when we go to the other place, the man who speaks for us, who has a duty to be impartial, who has that duty imposed upon him and who-I might remind hon. gentlemen-is the chairman of all four commissions in the United Kingdom. So it does seem to me that this would be an even better method of resolving the problem than any that has yet been suggested.
I would hope that this solution-which commends itself very much to me, I may say, as a good solution and one that would stand the test of time-might commend itself to all hon. members in every quarter of the house. I think there is one thing we can be sure of; that there would never be any criticism outside this chamber of the appointments that would be made by the presiding officer of this chamber. The only place where there could possibly be any criticism arise would be within our own ranks-and I would hope there would be none here. For that reason I am suggesting that if there was a consensus
Electoral Boundaries Commissions -I do not say universal approval, because you hardly ever get that in an assembly like this-on the part of hon. members that this would be a good solution, I would be very glad, if the hon. member's amendment should not carry, to put this forward as an amendment in the hope that it would carry. I am sure all hon. members will respect my feelings in this when I say that I would not wish it to be put forward unless there were a reasonable assurance that it would commend itself to the committee generally. I do not think we should do that in those circumstances, having regard to the office of the Speaker; and unless we are generally prepared to support this amendment I would not wish to put it forward at all.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the minister mentioned a moment ago a suggestion from Hon. C. G. Power. What was that suggestion? I think the hon. gentleman was getting away from it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: I think perhaps this would be an appropriate time to deal with it and perhaps the best way to deal with it would be to refer to it directly, just as did the hon. member for York-Sunbury some time ago.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: I think it was the hon. member for Royal.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Yes, it was the hon. member for Royal; I thought of Fredericton and got just a little confused. The suggestion was that there should be two assessors for each province, one of whom should be appointed on the recommendation of the leader of the opposition in the House of Commons and the other on the recommendation of the leader for the time being holding the majority in the House of Commons. That was the suggestion made in this particular bill. There was also another suggestion in an earlier bill that there should be two members, one appointed by the leader of the government and one by the leader of the opposition after consultation with the leaders of other parties in the house. They were the suggestions.
This brings me to the other alternative which also occurred to me.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: Before you get into that would you just answer this question. The minister did say that the Speaker in consultation with other members would make the appointment. Before the hon. gentleman leaves that phase of it, what has he in mind by consultation with other members?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
I did not have in mind that the amendment would contain anything about

Electoral Boundaries Commissions consultation with anyone. I said, as is the case in the United Kingdom and elsewhere, I understand, that there would in fact be consultation, but that I did not think we should attempt to prescribe consultation in the legislation. I think we should leave to the judgment of the Speaker what he should do about this matter, knowing that he will exercise his judgment in a sensible and practical manner.
The alternative suggestion which I had put forward was this, that we should leave the present bill as it is so far as the appointment of the commissions go.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
But I suggested we provide -and I hope the hon. gentleman will continue to say "Hear, hear"-that the leaders of other recognized parties in the house should have the right to appoint witnesses or assessors to be present at all the meetings of the commissions. Personally, I do not like this nearly as much but I am trying to think of every possible way in which we can do this so that it will at any rate definitely be open and aboveboard.
I recognize the force of the arguments used by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and others associated with him, by the hon. member for Fraser Valley and by some other hon. members earlier in this debate. They, too, represent in this house large bodies of electors, and it is only natural that they should feel that the heads of other political parties should not have a power of appointment which, even if it did not give them any advantage, would seem to exclude other hon. members who were equally elected to this house by the people of Canada.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the more experienced members of the committee will immediately recognize that this resolution is the one which usually precedes the introduction of the Canadian National Railways financing and guarantee bill. I may say that both as to form and substance the resolution is in keeping with the practice followed annually since 1952, with the exception of 1962 and 1963. As hon. members know, in those two years the annual financing and guarantee bills were combined into one bill late last year, but we are now returning to the practice of former years.
The bill which is foreshadowed by this resolution divides itself into seven main purposes and I shall attempt, with the indulgence of the committee, to explain those purposes briefly.
The first is to authorize capital expenditures by the C.N.R. in an amount not exceeding $155 million during the 1964 calendar year. As I understand it, this level of expenditure will run about the same as that incurred in recent years. There will be certain technical provisions within the bill authorizing payments not exceeding $72 million coming due between January 1 and July 1 1965, for capital expenditures incurred prior to 1965, and authorizing the C.N.R. to enter into contracts in an amount not exceeding $36 million for capital expenditures for the period January 1, 1965 and July 1, 1965.
The second main purpose of the bill will be to provide for the continued purchase by the Minister of Finance of the C.N.R.'s 4 per


cent preferred stock through to the end of the calendar year 1965. The 1962-63 financing and guarantee act extended to December 31, 1964, the expiry date of the authority granted by the Canadian National Railways Capital Revision Act, 1952, for the purchase of such stock up to a limit of 3 per cent of the gross revenue of the railway. In future years this provision and the other provisions of this annual bill might be affected by general railways legislation and a recapitalization of the C.N.R. While these matters are pending the bill recommends that the expiry date of this provision be extended to the end of 1965.
The third purpose of the bill is to extend until 1965 the moratorium on interest on the government loan of $100 million to the railway company authorized by the capital revision act, 1952.
The fourth purpose of the bill is a provision to increase to $680 million the limitation in the Canadian National Railways Refunding Act, 1955, placed on the authority to refund maturing or matured securities of the railway company. The limit at present is $480 million and it is desirable to increase this limit in order to give the railway company the authority to refund 5-J per cent Canadian National railway bonds maturing on December 15, 1964. These bonds, I might add, were exchangeable at the option of the holders on or before June 15, 1964, into an equal par value of 5J per cent bonds due December 15, 1971. Of these bonds, $190,445,000 were converted, leaving $8,555,000 still outstanding which are due to mature on December 15, of this year.
The last Financing and Guarantee Act extended the Canadian National's debt refunding limit by $250 million in view of the maturity of a like amount of Canadian National bonds on February 1, 1963. This issue was, in fact, refunded by a direct government loan to the Canadian National rather than by a bond issue by the Canadian National. I understand that there are no plans for a C.N.R. bond issue this year. However, it is considered desirable to have the added refunding authority equivalent to both C.N.R. issues in the event that debt management considerations ever pointed again to the advisability of C.N.R. bond issues.
The fifth purpose of the act will be to provide for the interim financing of Trans-Canada Air Lines during the first six months of the calendar year 1965 in an amount not exceeding $5 million.

One matter of concern, and perhaps the parliamentary secretary can tell us this, is whether, in the light of the proposed amendments to the Railway Act before the house at the moment, there have been any discussions or possible decisions regarding the refinancing of the whole Canadian National Railways debt structure? We are now getting up into the astronomical figure of $680 million as the limit for refinancing. I know it may be premature to discuss this question, but I think our attention has been drawn to what has been advocated by the railway management for some time, that is that the position of the Canadian National in relation to its debt structure should be subjected to a practical examination to ascertain whether or not it should be completely overhauled, and the railway given a chance to operate on the basis of current operations without having the albatross of these great losses of past years around its neck, which are related to the time when the system was welded together from a number of bankrupt lines. It is true that we have had this condition existing for 45 years, since Canadian National was organized. There must come before parliament a realistic appraisal of Canadian National Railways financial structure in order to eliminate this past debt.
Now, with regard to the appointment of auditors, that was gone into at some length last time. I do not suppose it really warrants anything being said on this occasion. I believe the auditors who have been appointed are competent people and that they were competent at all times. The less said at this time about what happened last year, the better. speechtext:
The measure before us is a routine one and there is no intention on my part of taking up a great deal of time or raising a variety of subjects. I would point out that the debate on this particular matter in previous years has on occasions been perfunctory and very brief, though at other times it has ranged widely, depending on the currency of interest in certain topics related to the Canadian National Railways and the C.P.R.
9962	HOUSE OF
Canadian National Railways The parliamentary secretary indicated to us that the whole question of debt reorganization is still up in the air. I think ministers of transport in governments since 1962 have been, 1 will not say less than candid, but less than informative about the attitude and intentions of the administration in this regard. I know the Minister of Transport was in the railway committee when this issue was raised last summer, and he gave a general indication that the government was considering favourably the proposals which had been put forward. He may recall that I put on the record of that committee some very strong criticisms by the C.P.R. and some of the trucking associations of the proposal for refinancing put forward by Canadian National. In doing so I had no intention of supporting this criticism. It was done, rather, to elicit from the president of the C.N.R., Mr. Gordon, a public rebuttal, if you will, of the C.P.R. charges. The C.P.R. feels of course that in any financing of the C.N., and any refinancing in particular, its main competitor is being given a tremendous advantage.
It has been my contention that whatever his merits in some areas as president of the Canadian National Railways, Mr. Donald Gordon has failed in the financial sphere of railway management. I have made this point before, but I will bring it up again. When the royal commission on transportation made its recommendations in the early '50's, Mr. Gordon was convinced that with the refinancing of the C.N.R. the railway would very soon be in a surplus position and would never have to worry again about the size of its debt structure, or about the repayment of those debts and the meeting of its other obligations from year to year. The position of the C.N.R. did improve and there were a couple of years when the railway did show a surplus; in one year it was a big one; in another it was not so big. The other cry was that the whole railway had to be rehabilitated; there had to be central traffic control and new equipment of all kinds.
It was in those years of the middle '50's that the annual bill which came before us began to escalate. It is almost fantastic, when you begin to consider it in detail, the massive capital expenditure by Canadian National since 1954. Mr. Gordon was wrong in his opinion that the refinancing which followed the report of the royal commission on transportation in 1950 would put the C.N.R. in a viable economic position vis-a-vis its competitors. He was wrong again when he argued


that the rehabilitation of the physical structure of the C.N.R. and the use of the most modern transportation methods would put the railway into a viable economic position and enable it to carry its debt.
Despite an increase in productivity, despite the decreasing cost of moving freight a ton mile which has resulted from all this tremendous expenditure, the position of the C.N.R. has really not improved. And so, after being wrong twice, Mr. Gordon comes up with his third major proposition since he became president of the C.N.R., namely that the debt structure should be completely reorganized. Figures have been mentioned running all the way from $690 million to $850 million. He has been most thorough in the proposition he has put forward. He elaborated it fully and clearly as long ago as 1961. He did so with particular thoroughness in 1962 and there were repetitions in 1963 and 1964. With all the discredit one may wish to place on the House of Commons, and the hesitation which a government may feel about trying to get a complicated measure such as this before parliament, this is a very bad show on the part of the administrators in the Department of Finance and the Department of Transport, and on the part of ministers over the last three or four years. It is a reflection upon them that it has taken so long for this debt reorganization to be handled and dealt with. In a sense, the kind of measure we have here would never have been necessary, or necessary in this particular form, if action had been taken on this more fundamental question.
I think it is our duty as members of the opposition to carp about this state of affairs, to criticize, to suggest that if Mr. Gordon has a case for debt reorganization, surely he has made it and made it again and again in the course of the last few years. I am very interested in this because the subject of debt reorganization fits into a much wider context. Recently there was a brouhaha in connection with run-throughs on the Canadian National, All across the country there was editorial criticism. Writers of editorials talked about "getting in the way of efficiency" on the part of the C.N.R. Well, if objection to a run-through affecting tiny little places like Nakina and Wainwright is getting in the way of efficiency, what about holding up of a question involving between $600 million and $850 million by the Departments of Finance and Transport?
How are those of us in politics who are aware that the C.N.R. is a crown agency to

react when we seem to be dealing on the level of $10,000 or $50,000 saved here or there in the name of efficiency while, at the same time, we have this kind of ball-up? And 1 think it is one, when the highest paid head of our largest government agency makes a serious and detailed proposition repeatedly, within the general context of tremendous change in the industry, change which affects the workers; within the context of other changes promulgated by the Railway Act which has been placed before us, which would alter the whole structure of freight rates in this country, something which would change the sacred cow and its ramifications in western Canada, which would lead to a massive abandonment program and which carries within it subsidies amounting to more than $1 billion in ten years. Nothing is done to deal with those important recommendations. Once again we come up with the traditional bill and we do not have the story before us relative to this question of the debt reorganization of the C.N.R.
I am not trying to put this out of focus or to distort it. But this is a very serious thing. I have heard all this nonsense-I like to call it garbage-about the MacPherson commission taking an over-all look at the railway picture. Damn it all, Mr. Chairman; it did not. There were a number of things it was specifically excluded from looking at, and it was not an over-all look at the transportation picture or an over-all look at all the railway problems.
I am not quarrelling with many of the recommendations, particularly the recommendation that a national transport council should be created. I think it attempted to prescribe, in the main, for the problems that the railways face; but it did not go into this whole question of the debt reorganization of Canadian National Railways; it did not go into the relationship of Canadian National Railways to the government or to the House of Commons. This bill, and the way these measures sort of march in in part and are delayed and held up, is an indication to me that we very, very badly need a good minister of transport. Maybe we have got one; I don't know. Maybe the present minister is the one we need. But surely we need a minister of transport who could get on top of all these matters, somehow get them into the House of Commons in some correlation and get them through in a complete legislative program-if you want, a session devoted to transportation problems. But it seems to me we peck here and pick there and get a
Canadian National Railways little bit, and always it seems we are behind, in legislative terms, as to what the railways, the shippers and everybody else seem to want and need out in the country.
This is true not only for the railways but it is true for air. You know, Mr. Chairman, the fandango we have had over air transport policy in the last while, including colourful little gallops across the television screen with the present Minister of Transport, and charges here and charges there. One minute we feel T.C.A. and C.P.A. might amalgamate and the next minute we are getting balloons,
I suppose, lifting with suggestions that no, it is a new kind of co-operation; and lately we have had the balloon that really in the air transport field the private carrier and private enterprise seem to be the answer. All I can say is that there is a considerable element of confusion, particularly in policy terms. This is not a major bill. We support it. In many ways we are not capable of arguing a great deal against it; but that is largely where it stands.
I have one suggestion to make, Mr. Chairman, that is not relevant to the bill but is directed to the Minister of Transport and the representatives of the Department of Finance. It is that in future, if we have to have more bills of this kind, they be sent to the public accounts committee where we would have the advice and guidance of the Auditor General. It is quite apparent that the Auditor General has views in this regard. I do not know how far he would like his arm to reach in assisting parliamentarians, but I have certainly had the impression from his comments about the C.B.C. and other crown agencies that he feels-and I certainly have felt, as a member of the committee at the times I have been a member of it-that the committee and the Auditor General together can do a good job in taking a look at these financial requirements of great agencies: I think this bill in particular is one that could go to the public accounts committee, be handled there very quickly and come back with more intelligent treatment, analysis, comment and recommendations than we can provide in this chamber, with the way the bill moves through it.
The last point I wanted to make in connection with the bill relates to the position of Air Canada as it seems to be involved in the C.N.R., with the C.N.R. as the financing agency. It is a very minor point, but it seems to me it is about time, in terms of the maturity of Air Canada as a company and because of its financial abilities, and that at least in the
9964	HOUSE OF
Canadian National Railways foreseeable future it seems to have a revenue possibility that is excellent, the government considered allowing it to make its own financial arrangements completely by itself, rather than operating through Canadian National Railways. I know that at the present time this is just a service that is offered by Canadian National Railways and there are no strings to this; but it seems to me that in the interests of clearness, even if it is just to stop the annual question in our parliamentary committee that examines the C.N.R. and T.C.A.-which indicates the confusion of all members of parliament about this-we might achieve something by making that separation.
There is one point about Canadian National Railways and all other crown agencies of this kind that has always bothered me, and I know the Minister of Transport has spoken about it a number of times. I refer to the boundary line between administration and policy, and the whole question of what rights or responsibilities fall upon the House of Commons and its members with regard to the crown agencies. The difficulty we have is to ascertain where administration stops and policy begins; there is a grey area here. The minister reports for Canadian National Railways and reports to Canadian National Railways when issues are raised in the house. The railway reports to him when it has certain matters to raise aside from the financing. Yet we are never very sure what the position of the House of Commons itself is with regard to this question. I can underline this point by the fact that it does not seem to matter, when we review the annual report of the C.N.R., whether any report comes back to the house from the committee with any recommendations. It just seems to be a routine that we go through, which recognizes that there should be provided some sort of a talk forum where we can probe the president of Canadian National Railways; but it suggests to me that we actually have no real power to make recommendations with regard to policy; that all we can do, in a sense, is advance ideas and we really cannot put forward policy recommendations.
I would suggest that the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Transport between them -particularly in connection with very large expenditures such as are covered in this bill and those they bring forward regularly- might consider this problem and see if they cannot provide us with a clear indication as to the rights of the House of Commons, or parliament, if you want, as an institution to examine, scrutinize and recommend in connection with these two very important


agencies, C.N.R. and T.C.A. I hope the bill has a speedy passage today, Mr. Chairman, and I hope that at least one or two of my comments may have found some response or echo with the Minister of Transport. As I say, it is not his bill; but some of us are living in hopes that he may be that good Minister of Transport that we have dreamed about.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, ISSUE OF SECURITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, every year a bill is introduced to authorize the Canadian National Railways to make certain capital expenditures allowing them to provide for some financial needs. The amount for the year 1964 is $155 million. As the year 1964 is almost ended, even though the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) asks us to accept this expenditure for 1964,1 believe that the greater part of this amount has already been spent and that we are only called upon to approve it in principle.
On the other hand, the farmers throughout this country will not even receive the sum of $80 million in subsidies. None the less, we know that agriculture constitutes an urgent problem. I quote those figures in order to point out that the federal government should spend the money of Canadian taxpayers more judiciously.
We are not told why those $155 million are needed. Naturally, only the total amount is mentioned; but I am somewhat concerned about the fact that this amount of money is handed over to the Canadian National Railways which can spend it in any way it chooses, while we know that for some years the C.N.R. has been invading a field of operations for which it was not intended in Canada. Let us examine more specifically its intrusion in the field of trucking.
There is in Canada a very well organized industry, which carries on business efficiently, gives work to thousands and even tens of thousands of Canadian citizens who pay income tax, which allows Ottawa to collect substantial amounts in company profits; it is the trucking industry. The Canadian National Railways, and not the "truckers", were intended to weld the various sections of the country. The C.N.R. has in the last few years gone into the trucking business, while private industry was well able to give adequate service in this field.
It is thanks to government income taxes, the citizens' income taxes and also taxes levied on trucking concerns, that the C.N.R. has started to compete with the trucking industry. Taxes collected from the trucking industry are handed over to the C.N.R., which uses

that money to compete with the trucking industry which was operating to the satisfaction of all.
Out of the funds which we are now asked to vote, what amount will be used by the C.N.R. to purchase trucks and to set up truck routes throughout Canada, in other words, to compete with the Canadian trucking industry?
It would certainly be interesting to know that, because if we are asked to vote millions of dollars to enable the C.N.R. to compete with private enterprise, the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance might as well know that we cannot go along with that. However, if the Canadian National Railways intend to use those funds to improve other services they operate exclusively, then it will be more acceptable.
The C.N.R. have a deficit of approximately $60 million a year and in addition, they get an additional amount of about $88 million during the year in the form of subsidies and grants of all kinds. But since subsidies are being paid to the C.N.R. for the transportation of feed grain under the pretext of enabling farmers to pay less, why not pay the same subsidies to the trucking industry? As a matter of fact, for instance, a farmer of the Saguenay-Lake St. John district who wants to buy feed grain will have to get it in Montreal in order to take advantage of the grants paid to the C.N.R. to reduce his cost price, because there are no trains running between Montreal and Lake St. John, and the trucks serving this run do not get similar subsidies. Then, the farmer will pay more for his feed grain because subsidies are only granted to assist one and not all transport companies.
I should like to submit to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) who proposes resolutions to approve C.N.R. expenditures, that the C.N.R. has an important role to play, that of linking together the various parts of the country. This is very important. The C.N.R. could be a determining factor in the economic development of our country but it would not be desirable that every action be taken to the prejudice of private enterprise or other segments of our economy, as is the case today, for instance, against the trucking industry.
It is true that the Minister of Transport has not been at the head of that department for very long, but I think that he should delve more deeply into the matter when discussing the part the C.N.R. should play and its
Canadian National Railways possible illogical competition with private enterprise in various fields.
This is what I heard the president of the C.N.R., Mr. Donald Gordon, say at a sessional railway committee meeting; "As president of the Canadian National Railways, whenever I am able to make a 5 per cent profit, I shall do so." That is an excellent aim, because this is a crown company for which he is trying to make as much profit as he can. He is working in the best interests of Canadian citizens as a whole. On the other hand, it must be said that this should not be done at the expense of other areas of our economy, because it does not make sense to improve one field to the detriment of another.
It is the responsibility of the Department of Transport to make sure that improvements in certain sectors are not made to the prejudice of others, but that as much co-operation is given to each of them.
That is not what is happening today. The Canadian National Railways compete strongly with the trucking industry as well as with the hotels and travel agencies, etc.
Mr. Chairman, I believe the minister should ask the directors of the Canadian National Railways to stick as much as possible to the aims for which they were established and to stop meddling ceaselessly into fields over which they do not necessarily have jurisdiction.
The proposed resolution mentions also:
-and to raise the limit on the Canadian National Railway Company's authority to refund matured, maturing and callable securities from the present level of $480,000,000 to $680,000,000.
I am of the opinion that this is an indication of the refinancing of the debt of the Canadian National Railways of which Mr. Donald Gordon, the president of the company, told us about for quite a while.
In this connection, I should like to ask the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) or the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Pennell) if, prior to going ahead with this refinancing, the whole matter will be referring to the railway committee.
Mr. Chairman, I think the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance did not hear my question as he was talking with the member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Choquette). I would draw the attention of the member for Lotbiniere to the fact that this is no time to ask for patronage from the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance; he should let him listen to all the questions we are putting to him.

Canadian National Railways
Mr. Chairman, my question was this: Could the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance tell us if before undertaking the refinancing of the C.N.R. we will have an opportunity of discussing the refinancing procedure in the standing committee on railways, or any sessional committee, so that we may hear witnesses who are interested in this refinancing or affected by the effects it would entail?
We are being asked today to approve an increase in the C.N.R. appropriations when we know that the money, or at least a large part of it, has been spent and that C.N.R. deficits are met, in one way or another, by the government. Although this approval is only a technicality, an approval after the fait accompli, I would nevertheless ask the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance to tell the president of the C.N.R. that even if we are voting money in this way, without knowing why, we would still like to have some assurance that this money will not be spent on trucking facilities to compete with a private Canadian industry which is doing quite well.
Mr. Chairman, even if we allow the C.N.R. to increase by $200 million the maximum amount of securities due or to become due which it may redeem, we think the matter should nevertheless be referred to a committee before C.N.R. refinancing begins.

Resolution reported and concurred in.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Pickersgill (Minister of Transport) moved
subtopic: IMPLEMENTATION OF AGREEMENT RESPECTING RAILWAY RELOCATION
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. S-33, to incorporate the Ottawa Terminal Railway Company.
He said: Mr. Speaker, if the house will agree, I have asked my hon. friend, the member for Russell (Mr. Tardif) to speak on this bill because the terminal is to be located in his constituency. He has familiarized himself with the bill and I know he could give a better explanation than I.

subtopic: IMPLEMENTATION OF AGREEMENT RESPECTING RAILWAY RELOCATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish I were as familiar with the bill to the extent the minister has given me credit. Not necessarily because of my efforts, but because it is logical that these improvements be placed in a proper setting, the new terminal will be located in my riding.
The purpose of the bill is to implement, with regard to the incorporation of a terminal railway company, the agreement for the relocation of railways in the Ottawa area dated October 17, 1963, between the national capital commission, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and the Canadian National Railway Company. I think it would be wise to give a few brief historic notes of how this came about.
The first commission that was appointed for the purpose of studying the railway problem in the capital city was established about 60 years ago when Sir Wilfrid Laurier was prime minister of Canada. At that time it was thought necessary to make plans to relocate
fMr. Pickersgill.]

the railways and to eliminate the circulation of railroads in and out of the centre of Ottawa, if the capital were to grow as it should. For that purpose a report was prepared by a commission in 1899. It was called the Ottawa improvement commission and, though it did not make a final plan it did make some recommendations that were incorporated in the last plan submitted to the national capital commission and the federal parliament. The plan I refer to is one involving the relocation of railway lines and their terminal.
In 1915 what is know as the Holt report was made, and confirmed what had originally been reported. Unfortunately the first world war stopped the implementation of this report and the plan was postponed for a period of about 20 years. At that time the national capital commission, which was interested in the development of a federal area, revised the plan because of the problem caused by the added traffic of railways in and out of the city, and again recommended to the federal government that the recommendations included in the original report be implemented. The railway and terminal facilities serving the city of Ottawa created many problems and at that time it was found that it would be logical to cure these things by implementing the report that had been made.
I know that hon. members who are here regularly, and who probably have been here longer this session than they have been before, realize that there are many problems created by the Ottawa river, the Rideau river, the Rideau canal and the fact that the city of Hull which is separated from the city of Ottawa uses these facilities provided by the central station. Not only do the comings and goings of trains in greater numbers create problems, but also depressed areas are created surrounding the tracks. About 1938 it was decided we should go about implementing this plan with greater speed. However, the second world war intervened and again delayed the implementation of the plan.

I hope members of parliament will understand, as I do, that even at this late date it is better to start immediately.
For this reason an agreement has been reached by the national capital commission, the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National Railways so that the construction of the projected terminus may be started right away.
Specifications are ready. The ground is being prepared. Nothing, therefore, could

prevent the carrying out of this program so that the necessary agreements may be signed by January 1, 1965.

I know hon. members will realize it is imperative that this be done as quickly as possible if we are going to cure some of the problems that now exist and which should have been cured many years ago. These plans have been delayed because of wars and other happenings. The relocation plan is now progressing. The Canadian Pacific and Canadian National Railways are going to be shareholders in this new terminal. It is planned that this terminal will be situated about a quarter of a mile from Hurdman's bridge and about two miles from the parliament buildings. It is planned also to construct a route with four or six lanes, I am not sure which, from the new terminal to the Chateau Laurier or the centre of the city. If we are going to have the terminal constructed according to the schedule that has been decided upon, it is important that this bill be passed by the house. I would ask hon. members to do so now.

subtopic: IMPLEMENTATION OF AGREEMENT RESPECTING RAILWAY RELOCATION
speechtext:
The concern I have with the bill is really the objections that have been raised to it by the trucking interests. I do not know what substance there is in them, but I assume the minister or the hon. member for Russell have seen those objections and have a clear answer for us. I think the general assumption would be that this would be a non-contentious bill in that it is really a follow-up on the consultations for the creation of industry and transport and for the betterment of our national capital's appearance.
According to the truckers, if this new terminal company is given the powers which seem to be apparent in one of the clauses, the terminal company can initiate trucking and transfer services and provide total warehouse services. One can understand their concern. There are a couple of points I should like to make in connection with the bill before us at this stage. The first has some connection with a point which was made by the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher). I refer to the powers which are granted to the company to provide terminal facilities.
The railways have been slipping into certain practices in terminals in various cities in Canada which have had a serious effect on local cartage companies. As you know, Mr. Speaker, the railways have got into the road transportation side of distribution to a considerable extent. Not only have they got into interprovincial, long range trucking but they also carry on local trucking operations. I am aware of instances where the railways have engaged in what might be called loss leader practices by offering to distribute goods arriving at terminals at rates which are much lower than the economic rates in effect through the local cartage companies. The rail-


ways are in a position to do this, because in their entire operations these cartage losses boil up into a general soup of losses against which are provided certain subsidies. True enough, the C.P.R. does not operate at a loss but it is able to offset losses connected with some of its terminal activities through subsidies which exist for freight rate equalization and so on.
I am wondering whether this bill will not encourage the practice to which I have just referred. Clause 10 of the bill gives authority for the provision of terminal facilities and there are any number of powers granted in this connection. I should like the minister to tell us whether it is the intention of the railway companies to engage in this practice of undercutting through the use of terminal facilities. The local cartage companies would be most surprised if they were suddenly to find that the Ottawa Railway Terminal Company had turned into one of their chief competitors to such an extent that they were losing a large proportion of their business.
After all, we should seek to ensure that local businesses are strong and flourishing. There is no point in granting large companies the power to engage in certain activities just for the satisfaction of putting local enterprises out of business. I know there is a very arguable case for the railways endeavouring to run an efficient operation. We all say three cheers to that. But what is the over-all price we shall be asked to pay to create this efficient framework, this efficient operation? The purchase price may be somewhat too high.
This is the main observation I have to make. Perhaps as we go along, as we get to clause 10, we can get some further information.

There are one or two points I wish to make. First we should like to know how much this relocation of the terminal in Ottawa will cost the federal government, and ultimately the taxpayers of Canada. This question has been asked before, and I presume the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) is prepared to answer it.
I do not really have any objection to the setting up of this Ottawa Terminal Railway Company for the purpose of relocating the railway terminal, in other words moving it from the downtown area to a location somewhere in the constituency of the hon. member for Russell (Mr. Tardif). But if the House of Commons decides this is a desirable action to take, the government should be prepared

to offer at least some kind of co-operation to those other cities in Canada which want to do exactly the same thing. I know that the city of Calgary has been attempting to enter into negotiations with the Canadian Pacific Railway to move its terminal from the downtown area to the outskirts of the city, thereby making available for commercial and industrial exploitation a very large area which is now being used for switch yards, freight terminals and so on.
I think the three prairie provinces, which are now handicapped because of the provisions of the statute of 1881 exempting the railways from paying taxes on their main lines, are entitled to equal consideration when they wish to proceed with this kind of redevelopment within their city limits. After all, the provisions of this bill, if you read the memorandum of understanding made between the national capital commission, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and the Canadian National Railway Company, require under clause 22 of the memorandum of understanding:
The commission will pay all costs and expenses incurred by the National Railways, Pacific Railway and Terminal Railway
(a) in development and preparation of plans, specifications, deeds, surveys, descriptions, applications and agreements;
The commission will also be required to pay all the costs in effecting the transfers of land referred to in this memorandum, including registration fees, land transfer taxes and municipal taxes that have been paid for any period after the land has been vacated or operations thereon abandoned by the railway, whichever is the earlier. The national commission is also required to pay all the costs in carrying out any other work that the railway companies may be required to do as a result of this memorandum or that the commission may lawfully require the railway companies to perform. We know that the national capital commission gets most, if not all, of its funds from the federal government, and it certainly seems to me that because the federal parliament is now disposed to paying huge sums of money-we do not know exactly how much it would cost, but I presume it would cost several millions of dollars to relocate the railway terminal in Ottawa to, if I may put it this way, dress up the city and make the downtown area more attractive, perhaps to have a more efficient and attractive railway terminal some place away from the downtown area in Ottawa-the federal government
Ottawa Terminal Railway Company should also be disposed to taking the kind of action that would be necessary in order that some of the cities in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta may also do this.
We know that because of this statute of 1881 the railways have acquired certain lands that are classified as main lines within the downtown area of cities in these three provinces, which gives the C.P.R., and I presume also the C.N.R., a very strong bargaining position in effecting any transfers of land with the end result of enhancing downtown areas. I do not want to speak for very long on this matter but, as is well known to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill), to the government and particularly, I might say, to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon), the premiers of the three western provinces have made representations to the Minister of Finance and to the government to have this statute of 1881 repealed so they can be on equal ground, if you want to call it that, and can bargain from a position equal to that of the railways. We know there has not been any action taken by the government to give effect to the representations that have been made. As a matter of fact the premiers of the three western provinces have made at least one, and I think more than one, trip to Ottawa to meet with the government and lay their case before them; and so far no action has been taken.
It seems to me that to be fair these three provinces ought to have some action taken by the federal government to remove this discriminatory statute that does in fact exempt the main line of the railways in only those three provinces; because after all, in all the other parts of Canada railways do have to pay taxes on their main lines. I believe that if we are prepared to spend several millions of dollars to remove this terminal from the downtown area in Ottawa to some place on the outskirts, we ought at least to ask the government to take the necessary action so that those three western provinces may also proceed in their negotiations with the railway company, and do exactly the same thing in some of the cities where there has been an expressed desire to enhance the downtown area by moving out the railway terminal and some of the side tracks that are there. When we get to the committee stage, Mr. Speaker, I want to ask some more questions along this line, but I raise these points now so that the minister may prepare himself to answer some of them.

Mr. Speaker, I know there are reasons why the station in Ottawa should be moved out into the country, and perhaps not the best one is the fact that the hon. member for Russell (Mr. Tardif) represents the new location of that station. But I wonder if we have really weighed the reasons for moving this station and whether it is to the advantage of members of parliament, people who deal with the government of the nation, or even the people of Ottawa themselves. We all know that people going to Montreal today-and I am told that most members are well aware of this; maybe they will not say anything

very seldom fly to that city. It takes longer to go to the airport here and from the airport at the other end than it does to get on the train a block from the parliament buildings and arrive downtown in the heart of Montreal. People coming into this national capital can come in one of three ways. If they wish to fly, they land at Uplands airport, a number of miles out of town, and find themselves, after a long, very rough taxi ride, in the downtown area. Those that come by car of course have many ways in which to get into what is a confused city for tourists; but they eventually find their way downtown to where they wish to do business, particularly those interested in the government aspect of this city. But those who come by train do not have any trouble in getting to the downtown part of Ottawa and usually-and fortunately, compared with most other cities-are able to leave the station and be in the downtown section or this area in a short period of time.
I am well aware that Charlotte Whitton wants to use this little area down here for a theatre; she has said so on numerous occasions. But I really could not care less what she wants to do with it. I, as a traveller coming into Ottawa for many, many years, have always been very happy with the fact that the railroad went downtown; that it was in the major section of the city, and I have always considered this to be a big advantage to anyone coming into Ottawa to do government business. It is not difficult to explain to people how to get to the parliament buildings if they arrive by train, because when one walks out of the station he can see them. I am quite well aware that we are going to have a new edifice out on Industrial avenue,


but to get to Industrial avenue means a long bus ride or, if one is coming to the city, a very confused trip by taxi or other means to get downtown to the business section.
I would be opposed to the railway moving the station out of this area. In my opinion they have some responsibility to the public that travels on the railroad, although there has certainly been less regard for the travelling public over the last few years than there has been to other revenue inducing parts of their enterprise. I am doubly surprised at this bill and I think I have support across the country in violently opposing a move to make the Canadian public pay for closing down the station in the downtown section of Ottawa, where it has been located since it was constructed, and relocating it out in the country. I cannot think of anything more silly than having one of our major transportation connection lines moved from a very advantageous position as far as the seat of the national parliament is concerned-it is only about a block away-to some place a great many miles out in the country. There is no point in talking about the roads which will connect it to the city because anyone who has driven on the roads in that area knows that a small car almost disappears during the course of the journey.
I am sure very little consideration has been given to the wishes of the Canadian public in this matter, particularly those of the public who travel by rail. If hon. members refer to the memorandum attached to the bill they will find the commission felt that in the interest of the national capital commission development plan it was advisable to relocate the station. I have discussed this matter with several members of the national capital commission when I have attended certain functions and have been able to raise the matter, and they just laugh and say there is nothing anyone can do about it. And I think that is true. I do not think there is a thing in the world that I can do about this and I do not think there is anything the Minister of Transport can do about it either. I think this move has been in contemplation for some time and probably it will come to pass. However, I do suggest that those who in their wisdom many years ago brought the railroads into the heart of the city were providing a service to the travelling public which we are not giving consideration to now.
I realize that the railway could not care less about its passengers. Anyone who has travelled on the C.N.R. finds that the accom-

modation is lousy. He will find that sometimes there is no one on the train who can tell why the train is running six or seven hours late, which happens periodically. It is matters like this which illustrate that the convenience of the travelling public is not given any consideration. However, let me just say that personally I am violently opposed to the relocation of the station from where it is now to somewhere out in the country. I would think that every hon. member of this house would have a hole in his head to vote for something which is not in his interest, is not in the interest of his constituents who may be using this facility, and no hon. member should be stupid enough to provide the money to make such a transfer.
