Mr. Speaker, to adopt some well worn words, I did not intend to take part in this debate. But since the opportunity has arisen I do want to take a few minutes to express my views on this particular bill.
I have found myself wondering during the past two or three years whether this plan to relocate the union station away from the central part of Ottawa is a good and sound plan in its present context. I think there is no doubt that ten or 15 years ago, when railway trains were hauled by steam engines which were generally considered to be dirty for a downtown section of any city, because of the coal dust and other deposits they blew into the air, and with their noisy whistles disturbing people in the downtown section, there was a very good argument for relocating a railway station somewhere else than the centre of a city. However, there has been quite a change since then. Diesels are now used 100 per cent on all railways which use this station. These diesels are quiet and they are clean, so I think that the objection based on that particular approach, if there ever was one, has now disappeared. I wonder whether second thoughts might have been given to the situation which existed five or ten years ago when the plan was originally formulated.
The second matter I want to raise is this. It is a fact that the present location of the station is very convenient for the travelling public, not only for those who handle freight and express but for passengers who come into the city and find themselves immediately in the downtown section. I should not be surprised if not very many years hence we were wishing we had this station right down in the centre part of the city of Ottawa. There is everything to be said for keeping it where
Ottawa Terminal Railway Company it is, although objection might be taken to the appearance of the station. Frankly I do not see where relocation of the railway tracks will be of any benefit. At present they run along a natural break in the landscape, just by the canal to a large extent. There does not seem to be any logical reason for this change, except the fact that a larger and probably more desirable complex of buildings could be constructed further out.
When this plan was first proposed some years ago, somewhere around the time I first came here, I saw the plan which had been prepared by the national capital commission. At that time it looked like a good thing to get this dirty railway station and all the railway trains out of the downtown section. But those who travel by air know that it is becoming more and more inconvenient to get to airports and similar facilities on the outskirts of cities.
I am not going to go as far as the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) and vote against this bill. I am not an Ottawan, except to the extent that one becomes more or less a citizen of Ottawa after being here for a few years. Nevertheless I do express some very serious doubts about the necessity for establishing a whole new complex in a location which will require us to make use of buses, taxis and other less convenient methods of transport in order to reach it. I am not talking so much about the welfare of members of parliament here, because I do not think that those of us who are here should concern ourselves about this slight amount of inconvenience. However, this city is the focal point of the travels of a good many people in diplomatic service, industry, and commerce of all kinds, and I think we should do something to make it less inconvenient for them when they are called upon to use the station. Therefore I express this very slight protest at this entire situation.
I assume that serious consideration has been given to this proposal. Also there may be other factors of which I am not aware. But I think that if the present building were put in good shape we would be no worse off because we have railway tracks running alongside the canal than we would be by having a road, which I do not think would be any more convenient.

subtopic: IMPLEMENTATION OF AGREEMENT RESPECTING RAILWAY RELOCATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to say only a few words about this bill. This seems to be another step on the part of the railroad industry to, in one way or another, reduce services to the public at an

Ottawa Terminal Railway Company increased cost, without any real benefit to the transportation system. By accepting figures presented by railroad officials we are in the position of not knowing their goals, or even the direction in which they are moving.
Mr. Speaker, the various acts in respect of railway operations would lead us to believe that railway companies are established to provide services. That is apparently their main and ultimate aim. Officials of the C.N.R., in particular, have said on many occasions that they believe the only profit making part of their operations is the moving of bulk cargoes. When the situation reaches the point where that is the actual fact, I am sure these same officials will tell us that even that side of their operations is no longer profitable.
The ultimate result of the measure now under discussion will be the transporting of fewer and fewer passengers from and to the terminal facilities in Ottawa. I suggest that is the apparent present day trend throughout the country. It has appeared to the general public for a number of years that the aim of railway companies is to cut down on costs, and to effect increased savings, with the inevitable result of a lessening in the number of services provided. This move has led to proportionate reductions in revenue. At the same time the railway companies decrease their costs, services and general expenditures, they increase their capital outlays.
In relation to the present measure before us, the terminal is being moved from the centre of the city, causing a complete rerouting of present line facilities, and creating increased capital costs and decreased services, with the net result of a decrease in passenger revenue. I should like to know where this trend is likely to end. We as legislators must ask ourselves this kind of question. I do not have a bone to pick in respect of railway services provided here in Ottawa, but my contention is that this measure is just one more example of what railway companies have been doing during the past five, six and even ten years.
What do the officials of railway companies expect to accomplish by expending a great deal of money for rerouting present lines, and relocating terminals? Is the provision of a new decentralized elaborate rail transportation terminal going to increase passenger travel and passenger revenue? Will the measure now before us bring about a new agreement as to the use of the Ottawa terminal by the two railway systems now servicing Ottawa? Will the two railway systems be able to economize as a result of the adoption of this measure?

Mr. Speaker, the only logical answer to the questions I have posed is that this measure will accomplish none of these things. It may enhance the city of Ottawa in an aesthetic way. It will undoubtedly cause the removal of some unsightly track locations in the downtown area. Surely these unsightly locations could be improved without the necessity of a huge capital expenditure to move the passenger terminal from the centre of the city. Surely the same result could be obtained by a different and less costly method.
We have been told that the C.N.R. passenger traffic, particularly, and we assume this is at least partially true of the Canadian Pacific Railway, is decreasing, yet we are proposing under this measure to establish a railway terminal company which will be allowed to spend a huge sum on capital acquisition for the handling of passenger traffic to and from Ottawa. This is a small measure, but in view of these facts I think it should be considered seriously. It should be considered in light of the general trend on the part of transportation companies to cut down on service facilities in order to effect certain economies.
Mr. Speaker, many royal commissions have studied the question of railway operating costs. I do not intend to discuss this subject in depth at this stage, as it is very complicated and involves formulae in respect of costing maintenance and per mile passenger operations. The present measure is a perfect example of another means by which the railway companies generally feel they can cut down on costs. By moving their terminals to outlying areas I suggest they will lose revenue as the result of the loss of passenger travel because of the inconvenience and loss of service.
This result has been apparent time and time again in the case of highway construction on the fringe of towns and cities, and the decentralization of air terminals. One can visit almost any part of Canada and observe the construction of highways and airport terminals in areas some distance removed from the centre of cities. These decentralization operations are in time accompanied by a general move of other services from the centre of cities. In the case now under consideration I suggest it is only a matter of time before the new terminal is surrounded by housing and industrial developments. Time and time again we observe the construction of highways at the edge of small towns and cities, only to observe within a very few years that they are again bordered and surrounded by communities which have moved from original

downtown locations. I suggest in the present case within a short period of time the new Ottawa terminal will be encompassed by a heavy build-up of homes and industries.
The officials of the railways may believe that they are accomplishing something by this present measure, but I suggest they will accomplish very little as a result of the expenditure of this large amount of money, and I support my contention by the words of the officials of the company concerned. They tell us their passenger revenues are decreasing. Do they expect to increase passenger revenue by increasing the inconvenience to passengers and decreasing services?
Mr. Speaker, I have very little more to say about this measure, but I should like to point out as a warning that the present transitional trend on the part of railway companies, which is particularly apparent in the prairies, where rail line abandonments are being considered, will in one way or another cut down on services, thereby decreasing revenues generally to the point where it is no longer feasible to continue any attempt to provide these decreased services. I am wondering whether this situation is not once again evident in the case presently being considered.

In addition, I would also assume that the large volume of freight and the necessary space required for freight car trackage were factors in the desire to take steps to beautify the central part of the city.
I was somewhat impressed by some of the arguments advanced by the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters), and as he was speaking something else came to my mind, namely the conditions that exist in relation to the new terminal development in the city

of Montreal, where one can arrive comfortably by train in the heart of the city and have ready access to the places he may wish to visit either on business or on pleasure. I should like to deal with the points that have been raised by various hon. members. The hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) and the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert), raised points which I think could be discussed more properly when the bill is before the committee. Quite frankly, I should not like to attempt to answer them at this stage.
There is one point of a general character that I should like to make right now, particularly if the bill is to go to a committee. The powers that it is proposed to confer upon this terminal company, which is a company to be owned jointly by the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific, are powers that these two railways have separately and which they can exercise separately, I am advised, even if they were not given to the terminal company. They would not give the terminal company any power to engage in any general trucking or other services, but only deliveries from the terminal.
I think this is the point. It was suggested in the other place, I believe, that this terminal company should not be declared a work for the general advantage of Canada in respect of these particular services. My department took the view that it was sensible that these things should not be separated-that you should not put delivery services under provincial jurisdiction and the rest of the terminal under federal jurisdiction. And we were able to convince the hon. gentlemen of the other place of the soundness of this view.
Those are the main points with which I should like to deal, now. The others would be better considered in committee where we could be more precise about them. As to the points raised by the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Olson) and by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Lloyd), it is true that in most parts of the country the Canadian Pacific and the C.N.R., in respect to those lines of theirs which were once privately owned, are taxable, except that the Canadian Pacific has a statutory exemption from certain kinds of taxes in the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta, conferred by this parliament, and I believe in parts of Manitoba, conferred by the legislation of that province. It is also true that the premiers of those three provinces came to


Ottawa some time ago and made representations to the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) and myself seeking to have these privileges removed from the railways. We are giving the most earnest, I might almost say anguished, consideration to this particular matter at the present time and while this consideration is being given I do not think it would be very helpful for me to go beyond what I have said.
As for the question raised by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Lloyd), the government owned railways were the property of the crown and, as such, under the constitution were not taxable by any other taxation authority. The companies have made some ex gratia payments in place of taxes but I know there has been a good deal of dissatisfaction about this matter. I have no doubt whatever it will be reviewed when we come to deal with the big railway bill. Having said that, I do not think I should go beyond it because I am sure hon. members will agree that it is not really relevant to the measure before us, though I do not blame either of the two hon. members for taking advantage of this opportunity to raise the point.
Other speakers have given the benefit of their views on this bill, either pro or con. The hon. member for Portage-Neepawa (Mr. Enns) was pro. I am not sure which side the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett) was on. The others were con. The station is, of course, to be moved to a new site in the area where my hon. friend from Russell (Mr. Tardif) lives and which, he tells me, he can reach without any trouble in ten minutes, though it often takes 15 minutes to get from here to the station in a taxi. I know from experience that this more rapid movement is due to the Queensway, and even this will be much improved when the station is moved.
I think some of us have forgotten that the basic decision to move the railway was taken in a previous parliament and under a previous government. The decision was made and the house voted money for it over the years. Most of the tracks have been moved already and if we now decided that a wrong decision had been made we would have to reverse a process upon which parliament decided a long time ago. All this particular bill does is to establish a terminal company to carry out a decision made long ago by parliament. If we had not wanted that decision to be taken, we should have resisted it a long time back.
The first decisions in this connection were made before I was a member of the govern-

ment, and that goes back 11 years. At that time I did not think much of the idea. But the decision was made and a great deal of money has since been spent to carry it out. This bill represents, if not a final stage, then at least one of the later stages in that process. If we were to be tempted at this late stage to reverse that early decision we would want to look very carefully at what the cost would be, and I doubt whether many members, when they were in possession of all the facts, would wish now to follow a different course.
The whole question of relocation could more properly be discussed on the estimates of the national capital commission, but I do not see, if this bill is to go to a committee, why there should not be some examination of it there, too. In fairness to the railways-I am not their apologist but I do think one should have some regard for the facts in these matters-let me point out that the railways did not want to move at all. A lot of persuasion, a lot of arm twisting had to be applied to both railways before the move was agreed upon. The railways were conscious of the point raised by the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) and by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken) that it was probably easier to get passengers if they were located in the middle of the town. It was the town planners of the governments of the day, both the St. Laurent government and the Diefen-baker government, and this parliament which decided the railways ought to do this. And it was quite a hard job to get them to do it.

He said: Mr. Speaker, I am going to do something that I do not think I have ever done before in the house, and I hope I will never do it again. I am going to follow my notes pretty closely in dealing with second reading of this bill, because I had rather expected that my colleague and parliamentary secretary would be doing it, and he had to be absent this evening. While I think I have a pretty fair idea of the contents of the bill itself, I would like to put a little historical material on the record which I perhaps would not get absolutely right if I did not follow the notes rather closely.
There are, as hon. members know, three kinds of harbours in this country. A number of our greatest harbours are under the national harbours board. There are a great number of harbours that are under the direct jurisdiction of the Department of Transport. In between these two categories there are a certain number of harbours which are governed by harbour commissions, which could only in the past and up to the present be set up by separate acts of parliament. There are 11 harbours administered by harbour commissioners, appointed under individual acts of the federal parliament. These are Port Al-berni, Nanaimo, North Fraser, New West-
[Mr. Winch.)
minster, Winnipeg and St. Boniface, one of our greatest harbours-

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: LEGISLATIVE PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: LEGISLATIVE PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONS
speechtext:
-Lakehead, Windsor,
Hamilton, Toronto, Oshawa and Belleville. The original legislation setting up the harbour commissions at Toronto, Hamilton, New Westminster, North Fraser, Winnipeg and St. Boniface dates from the period 1911 to 1914; the remainder were set up at various dates between 1947 and 1960. This latter group of acts follows a more or less standard form, but it has been found that even the more recent acts need to be revised if certain policies which it has now been considered desirable to follow-and I think there has been nothing partisan about this-are to be applied.
The harbour commissions carry out functions which are initially the responsibility of the federal government and substantial financial contributions are made by the Department of Public Works to these harbour commissions through construction of facilities and dredging. In the course of improving surveillance and control of these commission harbours, it has been found by the Department of Transport that the old legislation needed to be modernized to take into account the increased pace of development of the last few years. In the case of the older acts, this is partly due to changed circumstances and changes in the pattern of shipping practices and freight handling. Certain changes in administration policy are necessary as a result of ad hoc arrangements made in the past, different treatment in different parts of the country, and some confusion and misunderstanding which has arisen once in a while in the management of these harbours. A consistent policy has now been evolved, particularly in relation to the sharing of costs of works in proportion to the ability of an individual harbour commission to contribute to its own development.
The more recent acts prohibit the use of revenue for capital works, although the commissioners may borrow for this purpose with the approval of the governor in council. This makes awkward the carrying out of the policy for the sharing of the costs of capital works. The authority of a commission with respect to harbour development requires more precise definition. The award of annual "surplus profits" to municipalities under the early acts, and to the federal government under more recent acts, has been found to militate against the initiative and enthusiasm of the local commissioners which is so necessary to an

effective harbour advancement and development. The ultimate goal of a harbour commission is complete financial independence with all administration, maintenance and construction being financed from harbour revenues.
For these reasons, it is proposed to enact a new standard act which would correct these flaws and which would permit the Department of Transport to exercise a reasonable degree of control over these commissions while maintaining as far as possible the advantage of local administration and local initiative for which these commissions are especially valuable. The bill provides for the creation of new harbour commissions by order in council which would also define the limits of the harbour and the authorities having power to appoint the members of a commission. Similarly existing harbour commissions listed in the schedule to this act could be brought under the standard act as circumstances warrant. This is the procedure now used to create or amend public harbours under the Canada Shipping Act.
It seems to me, sir, that this is the general explanation, but I should like to say a word about application. It is proposed initially to make this act applicable to new harbours but it is also considered that some of the existing harbour commissions will wish to come under the provisions of this standard act. I think, however, that entering into detail of that kind would be much more appropriate in the committee. I think I should make one general observation. I know hon. members are always somewhat reluctant to confer upon the governor in council the power to do things that in the past have been done by parliament; but I do really think this is one case where parliament can very well be relieved of a power which has often been shirked by governments in the past. Because these bills, being of a local nature, did not command priority and often got put off from year to year, these harbours were not developed as rapidly as they might have been had more speedy action been taken. The parliamentary control is completely maintained because the governor in council may not depart from the standard provisions; so that there is no power that can be given these harbour commissions which is not conferred by the act itself.
In addition, I may say that very exhaustive examination was given this bill in the committee in the other place. I appeared there and I think the representatives of all the harbour commissions interested also appeared and got a very good hearing. Several changes were
Harbour Commissions
made in the bill in the other place to meet the representations which were made, and to the best of my knowledge there is no feeling now on the part of any existing harbour commission that its position would be in any way affected adversely by the passage of the present bill.
For that reason, Mr. Speaker, and because I would not like to get a state of constipation, if I may put it that way, in the railway committee, I would hope that we could deal with this bill in committee of the whole and dispose of it this evening.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the surface this bill does appear to be somewhat arbitrary in giving the government power to take over the operation of any of the 300 harbours which might be affected, with the exception of the three taken out during the course of the bill's consideration in the Senate-namely, Toronto, Hamilton and Winnipeg-St. Boniface. The bill also permits the taking over of those commissions which are set out in the schedule to the bill. However, in assuming control of these harbours, if the government sees fit to take control, they also bear a certain amount of cost as well. Therefore it is fair to assume that the government will not rush in unnecessarily to take control of various harbours where the expenditure of money is involved.
There was a very long discussion of this particular bill in the Senate. In fact, the same bill was before the other place in the previous session as bill S-38, but never left the other place in the last session, after the exhaustive discussion which resulted in the harbour of the city of Toronto being excluded. The former bill died at prorogation of the last session.
Under the new bill now before us the harbours at Hamilton and Winnipeg-St. Boniface are also excluded. As the minister said, exhaustive consideration was given the bill in committee in the other place. That is true not only of Bill S-10 but also of the previous bill S-38. All the municipalities which wished to appear and all the harbour commissions had full opportunity to go through the provisions of this bill. Therefore, in spite of this initial reservation that perhaps there is too much arbitrary control, I think most of the objections to the principle and the detail have been settled and we will not oppose the passage of this bill.

subtopic: LEGISLATIVE PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill, or at least one part of it, caused a bit of a sensation last year when

Harbour Commissions
to the surprise of most of us, while it was before the Senate telegrams and letters suddenly began to rain upon us complaining about the bill. I remember that I spent two mornings or afternoons sitting in the Senate committee listening to complaints from Hamilton and Oshawa, and to representations from my own area regarding the views of the lakehead municipalities. I think that these objections have been met. Certainly at the time I could not really see what these people were worrying about, including the representatives of Hamilton and Toronto, but I assume they managed to convince the government that they were in a special kind of situation which should keep them free of the powers resting with the government, in this particular case with the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill).
There are two comments I want to make about the bill and about the harbour commissions. One concerns conflict of interest and political partisanship in relation to the commissioners themselves. The other is the matter of the revenues which a commission raises.
The conflict of interest is something which is extremely difficult to determine, but it does seem to me that it is something which needs to be kept very much in mind by the governor in council when making appointments. I want to give the minister an example. The Canadian National Railways, as the minister knows, is an agency to which he has some relationship, as well perhaps as having some power and influence over it. We had a situation where one of the government appointees to the commission at Port Arthur was an employee of the Canadian National Railways; at least that was my understanding. I am not saying there was anything wrong here, but there was only one commissioner there who did not have some interest in connection with the harbour. One was the head of the shipyards. Another was the head of an elevator company which was involved. Another was an employee of the Canadian National Railways, a very able engineer. Because of their backgrounds and, you might say skills, these men were excellent people from one point of view to have on the commission, but the suspicion was raised in more than my mind that it was rather unfair that these men should be there.
For example, there was a controversy at the lakehead over who should bear the cost of icebreaking in the slips and around the harbour. One of the solutions seems to have been worked out as the result of a visit by

the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp), representing the grain interests, and I think the matter has now been resolved. But one of the matters which caused a great deal of questioning and bitterness on the local scene was the fact if the lakehead harbour commission had become more deeply involved in financing and in paying for this particular form of icebreaking it would immediately have thrown suspicion on the representative of the grain trade who was on the commission, because naturally it was the grain trade who stood to benefit most.
I have tried to think of an amendment to the bill which would so limit the appointments, but it would be almost impossible to rule out the appointment of this sort of person. Yet this is a matter which must be kept very much in mind, particularly in terms of balance. From the experience on the lake-head scene, which I am sure is duplicated in other harbours which tend to have the same interest, I would say you are caught between the fact that such men do tend to have the most knowledge to bring to bear, but they also have the most interest in what is involved. It seems to me that a special onus is left on the government when making these appointments.
One of the other problems which arises in connection with appointments is the political affiliation or interest of the people who are appointed. The federal government cannot be sure as to what may be the politics of municipal appointees, but it is very obvious from experience both under a Conservative government and under a Liberal government that this is looked upon as some kind of minor reward or recognition for a party man. As a politician I have no objection to that on principle, but I would put it to the minister that this, along with the conflict of interest, adds to the view that people tend to look upon harbour commissions as a political agency of the government or as an arm of the government identified with the ruling party. If you are not in that party or the government you can take some comfort from this, because it is not a very pleasant situation for the Department of Transport to be in- that a local agency, with which it has such intimate connections, is looked upon as being a partisan group. Again, you cannot spirit it away with any kind of amendment.
I should like to put to the minister one of the things, judging by the situation at the lakehead and at several other communities of which I am aware, which would help matters considerably for the minister-al-

though I suppose it is his deputy, with some kind of political connection, who ferrets out people for appointment. The minister should deliberately try to make sure that the people chosen are not those who have a glaring, open or marked reputation for being political partisans. I do not want to leave the impression that I think, because individuals support a party, or are particularly loyal to a party, this leaves them with a bar sinister, but the fact remains that a member of practically any other party can probably see these difficulties and dangers more clearly than anyone else.
This is the kind of an agency or commission we cannot get at as members of parliament, acting as either individuals in our constituencies or as members in the House of Commons. We have really no power of scrutiny. All we can do is sound off with criticisms. It is for that reason I think the whole practice with regard to appointments of harbours commissioners should be considered very seriously by the present minister and his deputy in an attempt to see whether they can establish, perhaps not any fixed rule, and certainly no regulations, but some sort of policy to take care of this conflict of interest in this partisan aspect. I do not know how possible such a thing is, but we know the present minister is not the least partisan of people, and I suppose his deputy, just as a result of the fact he has been at his job for so long, is both adept at and inured to compromise with a sort of a political reality, but I suggest to the minister that this might be at least an aspiration. I suggest that he examine this conflict of interest and this question of political appointment to see whether the difficulties that surround them can be circumvented by the appointment of people who have no conflict of interest and are not partisan.
The last topic I want to touch upon, Mr. Speaker, is the subject of revenues. Having read the lakehead harbours bill and this bill, I am not clear in my mind just how much freedom the local harbour commissions have to raise money. I do not know what is the pattern of their financing. Perhaps one thing we might gain by having this bill sent to a committee is some indication of the record of financing problems. I know there are financing problems and that the harbour commissions must obtain money. Since much of the money that has gone into harbours has come from the federal government, the federal government should have some control. I should like to know how much latitude exists for harbour commissions to make unilateral decisions, for 20220-632
Harbour Commissions
example that they are going to raise the fees for the use of the harbours without previous consultations with the government. It seems to me that the actual situation which exists is that tacitly, despite the powers given by the bill, commissions tend to look for and accept the advice of the minister of transport.
Again because this is not spelled out clearly, it seems to me that there may be a certain hypocrisy in the bill, in that the great powers for raising money which exist in the general and particular powers are really not as strong or powerful as we may think when we pass the bill.
The question I should like to leave with the minister is, since this is an over-all bill bringing a number of harbour commissions in this country within a single framework, whether it would be possible out of this single pattern to establish some kind of annual publishing of the reports of these commissions in some detail so that we will have a picture of their operations. I happen to know that these commissions publish their own statements, but it seems to me there should be a common format indicating statistics of revenue, traffic and expenditures, with a budget for the coming year. This might be very useful and should in no way inconvenience the commissions in doing the jobs which the powers given to them by the bill would indicate they are doing. That is really the only substantial request I make to the minister. Would he consider whether it might not be possible to have some kind of publishing of a common nature carried out. This may involve an extra cost upon the Department of Transport through the queen's printer, but it seems to me it would be a most useful thing.
One of the difficulties in trying to analyse harbour needs in this country is that the report of the national harbours board gives specific data only for so many harbours, and then only general data in respect of all the rest. I think the minister will recognize that the dominion bureau of statistics does not really pick up the slack and give a ready picture of the kinds of traffic, a summary of the facilities and revenue, and a general plan of the capital expenditure for various harbours. This would be something hon. members would find useful. Certainly I would find this very useful, as it would enable me to follow from year to year what is taking place.
It seems to me there is always some question in our minds when we have three or four patterns of administration of similar facilities such as harbours. We have the na-

Harbour Commissions
tional harbours board, and we are now going to have this schedule of harbours under this act. There are other ports which have harbour commissions but which will remain outside.
One of the questions repeatedly occurring has to do with a scale of expenditures, and the kind of facilities which should be provided. The minister may remember the controversy over who was going to pay for the provisions to extend the grain handling facilities at both the lakehead and Vancouver. One was under this kind of a commission and the other was under the national harbours board. The relationship of the government's role with respect to expenditures in this particular area has never really been settled clearly. I do not know where there is a more primary responsibility upon the government in relation to a harbour under the national harbours board than in respect of a harbour under this particular act, but certainly they are treated differently in relation to administration and financing, and their relations with the department are different.
I suppose we should really be asking whether it might not be practical to look forward to some future time when the national harbours board is the general administrator of all harbours. As long as there are three different kinds of harbours which handle a substantial amount of traffic there may always be the possibility of some kind of rationalization of the whole relationship of the federal government to them. I think the previous minister of transport deserves some congratulations for the fact that all the objections to this bill, which were many, disappeared a few months ago while he was still in charge of the department. I can only assume that since it took place under his regime he played some part in allaying the suspicions, and since we have not been congratulating him too much lately it might not be amiss to do so now.

subtopic: LEGISLATIVE PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a few remarks I should like to add to those made by the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) in connection with the bill. My first reaction was somewhat similar to that expressed earlier by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken), namely that we should look rather carefully at the suggestion that we put into the hands of the governor in council powers which heretofore have been exercised only through an act of parliament. However, I was satisfied at least partially by the explanation of the

Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill), that one of the results of the passage of this measure might be to facilitate the establishment of harbour commissions where otherwise they might not be established.
I should like to say to the minister that one thing for which I am always on the lookout is the development of a government policy to provide for a more satisfactory method of administering smaller ports than in my view has heretofore been devised. If the passage of this bill will help to facilitate that kind of development I want to say here and now that I am all for it, although I do not actually see anything in the bill to indicate definitely that its provisions contain the kind of solution which I should like to see brought about in respect of the administration of many of the smaller harbours.
I have only one harbour in my constituency which is administered by a harbour commission, the harbour of Port Alberni. If I may say so, this is one of the more important harbours on the west coast of Canada. In fact, according to some claims I have seen recently it is British Columbia's second harbour from the point of view of tonnage shipped, although I believe that the harbour commission in the constituency of the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Cameron) is inclined to challenge that claim.
Nevertheless, what I really want to say is that I have discussed the possible effect of the bill with the Port Alberni harbour commission and my understanding is that they are satisfied its terms will not adversely affect the operation of that harbour. There are one or two matters in connection with the provisions of the bill that I may wish to question when we get to the committee stage.
One of the advantages I have always felt arose out of the operation of harbour commissions established by an act of parliament, as has been the case up till now, was that out of their revenue surplus they did have certain funds, usually not too large in the cases that have come to my attention, which could be spent entirely at their own discretion. There have been certain advantages in this situation. I know that some works in the harbour of Port Alberni have been constructed in this way which might not have been constructed if they had required a vote out of public funds at the federal level. Nevertheless these works have added to the usefulness of the harbour.
I think I understood the minister correctly that in the future any harbour commission which is operating within the framework of

this legislation will have no such surplus funds, because any such funds will automatically go into the consolidated revenue fund after certain operating expenses and so on have been taken care of. This particular aspect of the bill raises some questions in my mind which I may wish to pursue further in the committee stage.
If I may sum up, Mr. Speaker, I hope we are moving in a direction which will facilitate the more adequate administration of smaller harbours. In my experience they have largely been left out of the picture from the point of view of creating an efficient mechanism for local administration. The result has been that there have been many headaches for the administrative officers of the Department of Transport, inasmuch as these habours are in most cases isolated from any direct, day to day supervision by these officials.

Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Lamoureux in the chair.
Clauses 2 and 3 agreed to.
On clause 4-Contents of proclamation establishing commission.

subtopic: LEGISLATIVE PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I should like to inquire about the thinking of the government in proposing that the number of members of a commission shall in all cases be not less than three and not more than five. There is nothing unusual in this proposal in itself but I raise the question because of the point I mentioned earlier when we were at the second reading stage with respect to the administration of smaller harbours. So far as the administration of smaller harbours is concerned, has any consideration been given to the possibility of setting up a modified form of harbour commission involving a single commissioner? There might not always be three suitable people available. Has the minister any comment?

subtopic: LEGISLATIVE PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I can make a very brief comment on that point. I think that a harbour that can be administered by one person should not have a harbour commission at all but should be in the third class of harbours I have mentioned. Unless a harbour is of sufficient importance and magnitude to warrant at least three persons being appointed, it does not seem to me there would be any advantage to be gained at all in removing it from the class of harbours 20220-632i

which includes the great majority in Canada and which are administered directly by the Department of Transport.

I will not quarrel with the minister on that point but I raise it because
I	think there is need for the development of a better mechanism for the administration of smaller harbours than I have seen up to the present time. I hope further consideration will be given to this matter.

subtopic: LEGISLATIVE PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONS
speechtext: As a matter of fact, it was thought when we were waiting for action on this legislation, we might put the harbour at St. John's, Newfoundland under a harbour commission under this legislation. subtopic: LEGISLATIVE PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, in connection with clauses 9, 10 and 11, but particularly 10, is it the intention that the government shall acquire the harbour facilities, that is the land, buildings and so forth, and transfer them to the commission or is it the intention that in most cases, the commission will merely administer the assets that are physically there?

subtopic: LEGISLATIVE PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONS
speechtext: There is no question of anything being taken over. In the case of existing commissions, the commission does own works in the harbour. In the case of any new commissions that would be established, I would assume any federal works in the area would be turned over to the commission.

subtopic: LEGISLATIVE PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONS
speechtext:
I want to raise a question with the minister in connection with the powers, particularly under paragraph (h). The minister may recall that there have been some proceedings against ships for dumping waste oil and other refuse. I understand these proceedings have been taken under the Criminal Code, although the harbour authorities may have provided the information for the charge. I want to find out whether this power under paragraph (h), and under the authority to establish police, could be used more effectively than seems to be the situation at the present time in relation to the few examples we have seen where the scale of fines against these shipping masters and shipping companies that have been dumping oil have amounted more or less to a pat on the wrist.
I wonder if the minister could tell us if there has been enough experience with this kind of harbour commission, with the problem of policing, discipline and good conduct of harbours, to indicate that they should assume more of the powers this section would seem to give them? I know I am getting rather indefinite, but what I am really asking is, does the practice up to now indicate there should be a limitation upon the policing and, if you like, the punishment powers of the commission in the sense of the present reality as against what seems to be the sweeping powers that are given under this particular clause?

subtopic: LEGISLATIVE PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONS
speechtext:
I think it is the general rule that commissions which are set up under a statute can exercise only the powers the statute itself confers. A commission could not make criminal law-at least I defer to the lawyers here, but I would think this most unlikely. They could only create the kind of offences that relate to the specific powers given to them. This is one reason their bylaws would have to be examined by the governor in council, so the Department of Justice would have a chance to look at them and make sure they were not purporting to make bylaws which could not have any legal validity be-

cause they had not had conferred upon them the power necessary to make the bylaw.

subtopic: LEGISLATIVE PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONS
speechtext:
I appreciate that comment. We have had two matters locally in which the commission has been involved and, in the opinion of some people, regrettably not sufficiently involved; one was the question of oil and the other relates to the right of the harbour commission police to deal with duck shooting and the carrying of firearms in the harbour area. One of the consequences in terms of public opinion on the local scene that I encountered with each of these instances was that the harbour commission and its police were damned if they did and damned if they did not. They were damned by some people for interfering with the shooting of ducks, and they were damned by other people because they had not taken sufficiently strong action in connection with the release of waste oil.
The point I really wanted to make to the minister hinged on how much encouragement, despite the fact of perhaps because of the fact, the government retains the scrutiny of bylaws, will be given to harbour commissions to sort of police and, in that sense, punish, the people who commit these actions? I suppose in the context of what we are doing here, this is a fruitless question. I am quite prepared to allow the clause to pass, but I should like to remind the minister and his officials there is a problem here that I am sure will be cropping up again and again.

subtopic: LEGISLATIVE PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONS
speechtext:
It does crop up a great deal. There are some very difficult questions because, as the hon. gentleman knows, sometimes the dividing line between what is regarded as property and civil rights and what is regarded as shipping is not an easy one to draw. I have just taken two examples at random. I understand it is the desire, as much as possible, to encourage these harbour commissions to maintain good order in their harbours, to see that everything that is properly within their powers is done and to avoid things like pollution, the dumping of garbage or anything of that sort.
I wonder, sir, if you could avoid seeing the clock if that were the wish of hon. members, for a few minutes so that perhaps we might conclude this matter.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 14-Commission may borrow and issue debentures therefor.

subtopic: LEGISLATIVE PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONS
speechtext:
I should like to ask one or two questions in connection with clause 14.

They may be related to clauses 14 and 15 which have to do with the powers of the commission in connection with the expenditure of money for capital and operating purposes. One of the questions which occurs to me is whether the passage of this bill will alter the pattern that has existed in the past in relation to the policy of smaller harbour commissions to make arrangements for capital expenditures by appropriations from the Department of Public Works for the construction of certain works such as wharves, breakwaters and so on. Second, what would be the effect of the operation of these two clauses on the ability of the commissions to construct minor capital improvements within their harbours without having to go cap in hand to parliament for an appropriation, or having to borrow money under terms which would involve payment of interest?

subtopic: LEGISLATIVE PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONS
speechtext: I think I can deal with those points very briefly. I should like to deal first of all with the points the hon. member raised on second reading; I am sure it might create a certain amount of misgiving if we were just to read the last three lines of clause 15. Perhaps I could deal with the relevant clauses together, as the hon. member did. It is not the intention of the governor in council to insist that any surplus which might be left over each year should be paid to the receiver general. Paragraph (b) of clause 15 (2) refers to the appropriation to the funded reserves of the commission of such amounts as may be approved; it is intended that these harbours should build up funds from their revenues and have them available for their own use. However, it is thought that if the funds become so large, and if they are based on capital works originally paid for by the taxpayers, the surplus, if it is to go to anyone, should go back to the exchequer which provided the capital in the first place. There is no thought whatever of trying to make large profits out of these harbours. As far as capital works are concerned, where revenue is sufficient the commissions are not restricted from carrying out capital works of their own; they do not need to come to us for permission. But many of these harbours are not self-supporting and are not likely to be. In these cases the Department of Public Works will share, with the harbour commission in providing the kind of works which would be provided in harbours of that kind if there were not a harbour commission.

subtopic: LEGISLATIVE PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONS
speechtext:
Let me be clear on this question of funded reserves. I took that expression to mean reserves to pay off the bonded in-
Harbour Commissions
debtedness of the commission. But a commission could build up a reserve out of which it could undertake direct capital works made possible by accumulated surpluses.

subtopic: LEGISLATIVE PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONS
speechtext: It is my understanding that that is also true. In fact it is for both purposes.

Clause agreed to.
Clauses 15 to 18 inclusive agreed to.
On clause 19-Expropriation.

subtopic: LEGISLATIVE PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONS
speechtext:
There is just one question I wish to raise with regard to this clause. I may have a technical mind, but there seems to me to be a problem here in connection with expropriation. The assumption is that anyone is prepared to sell for a price. The clause says:
A commission may.. .take or acquire lands... without the consent of the owner where it is unable to agree with the owner as to the price to be paid therefor-
The question which arises in my mind is this: Suppose the owner does not wish to sell at all, and there is no argument at all about the price. Would the clause be operative in these circumstances? It would seem that the words "as to the price to be paid" would be surplus. Someone might say merely "I will not sell", and there would be no power of expropriation.

subtopic: LEGISLATIVE PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONS
speechtext: I understand that the provision of the Railway Act which is applied by reference here is that the expropriation would only be legal if the property expropriated was essential for the railway. A railway could not expropriate for any other purpose. Therefore, by analogy it would have to be clearly needed for the harbour before this power could be exercised; and of course in case of dispute the courts would decide wheher it really was needed. Moreover, if any such expropriation can of course only be done with the consent of the governor in council. I think the hon. gentleman knows that there is always likely to be pretty strong opposition in this house, which would be very likely to bring up the grievance of anyone who really felt aggrieved in this matter, and that the governor in council would not act lightly.

subtopic: LEGISLATIVE PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not think my point was understood. My point is that the power of expropriation that the commission has is limited by the words "as to the price to be paid therefor". As I say, what is the situation where someone says in effect, "I do not want to sell"? There is no power

Harbour Commissions
of expropriation in such a case. That is my point. If there is an argument about the price, the commission may expropriate. If there is no argument about the price, and if the man just says. "I am not going to sell," there is no power of expropriation. This is the point that is not made clear in the bill.

subtopic: LEGISLATIVE PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I wonder if I could ask that this clause stand for a moment, in the hope of getting some legal advice from on high, while we go on with the other clauses. I have not any lawyers in front of me; I am not a lawyer, and I would not like to go very far in this field without advice. Perhaps we could stand clause 19.

subtopic: LEGISLATIVE PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, in respect of clause 30 I have been asked to have it made clear on the record whether or not the harbour commissions as listed in the schedule to the bill will remain free to continue under their present charters as established by the various acts of parliament unless there is agreement as to the provisions of both paragraphs (a) and (b) of subclause 2. In this connection I would think it appropriate that the minister, particularly because as I understand it in most, if not all cases a majority of the members of the harbour commissions are appointed by the government, should say whether or not it is the intention of the government to exert any influence upon the existing harbour commissions, either directly or indirectly, as to what action they should take to bring themselves under the terms of this bill; and, in reference to that section that has to do with municipalities, whether the government intends to make any representations, directly or otherwise, to the municipal authorities in connection with bringing existing harbour commissions within the framework of this bill.

subtopic: LEGISLATIVE PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONS

I can say, first of all, that I gave an assurance to the committee of the other place-if it is permissible to say that- that there would be no pressure whatsoever brought on any of these harbour commissions. They have acts of parliament. Unless they see some advantage in coming under this legislation there is nothing we can do for them. I do not think there is anything we should try to do to coerce them in any way. We feel that it will be apparent that there are certain advantages to them in coming under this legislation, but that is for them

to decide and not us. As for trying to influence municipalities either to establish harbour commissions or not establish them, I think that is something about which I have to be a little cautious in answering.

subtopic: LEGISLATIVE PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, may I say that I did not ask the minister about influencing municipalities in order to establish new harbour commissions. I was referring to asking the municipalities to co-operate in establishing-

subtopic: LEGISLATIVE PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONS
speechtext: Well, let me just say that that would be in an infringement of provincial rights which no Liberal government would contemplate.

subtopic: LEGISLATIVE PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONS
speechtext: In the case of one of the listed harbour commissions appearing in the schedule, I hope it will not be a condition of the provision of certain capital installations through, say, the Department of Public Works that it would be necessary to pass the appropriate bylaws and come under the great controls.

subtopic: LEGISLATIVE PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF HARBOUR COMMISSIONS
speechtext: I really do not think there would be any particular advantage to the federal government in doing that, even if we had any thought of doing it. The only thing is that there might be in some of these other statutes-I have not gone over them carefully in comparison with this bill-certain things we could not do for them under their existing legislation which we could do for them under the present legislation. There might be some advantages there. However, I do not think we would hesitate to point that out to them. Otherwise it is not our desire to try and impose any uniformity at all. We think this legislation is rather better than any of the existing acts and rather better from the point of view of the commissions, but that is for them to decide.
